paper.title: Systematic differences across evaluation schemes and educational choice
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement. The paper states only that 'The data used in the empirical analysis is a dataset put together from different administrative registers hosted by Statistics Denmark' (p. …

registers.name_in_paper: different administrative registers hosted by Statistics Denmark
assessment data: teacher scores and exam scores by subject-area in the grade 9 school-leaving certificate
pupil background data (gender, parental education, migrant background, family structure, number of children, parental income and occupation)
enrolment in education in the autumn after completing lower secondary school

registers.role: robustness check: survey-measured parental attitudes and preferences, and pupils' stated education choice

linkages: Data on pupil background is linked to assessment data via a personal registration number (p. 45).

Pupils are linked to siblings (families) so that sibling fixed effects can be estimated; the sibling sample consists of pupils with at least one sibling also graduating from grade 9 in the 2005-2009 cohorts (p. 46).

sample.universe: Pupils in public and private schools in Denmark (including efterskoler, independent boarding schools for upper secondary students, but excluding schools for students with special needs) completing grade 9
sample.unit_of_observation: Pupil-by-subject-area observation in the grading gap regressions (the datasets are stacked: for each student there is one observation per subject area); pupil in the educational choice regressions and simulations
selection_rules: Grading gap regressions: seven cohorts of pupils completing grade 9 in 2005-2011, roughly 400,000 pupils.
Only pupil-by-subject observations for which both teacher and exam scores are available are included.

Only subject-areas assessed by both teacher grades and exams in both periods are included; a small number of subjects where exams are optional and chosen only by a small number of pupils are excluded (footnote 14).

For the 2011 cohort, subjects where pupils were assessed by the national tests in grade 8 (Danish, Biology, Geography, Physics/Chemistry) are excluded, because external assessment results were available to the teacher before the final teacher grades were given (footnote 13).
Grading gap regressions are estimated separately by exam-score (ability) quintile; the robustness specification in Table 6 uses the full sample with the exam score as a continuous control.
Educational choice regressions: the five cohorts of 2005-2009, for which enrolment in the autumn after completing lower secondary school is observed.

Educational choice regressions are estimated on the sibling sample (pupils with at least one sibling also graduating from grade 9 in these cohorts), about one third of the total sample, separately for boys, pupils with low educated parents and migrant pupils, and by ability quintile.
Table 6 column 4 additionally excludes schools with fewer than five migrant pupils in the school-by-year cohort, which reduces the sample by almost 25%.
sample.period: Grade 9 cohorts 2005-2011 (grading gaps); 2005-2009 (educational choice and simulations)
sample.n_observations: 848,065 / 846,174 / 849,290 / 844,075 / 846,220 pupil-by-subject-area observations in ability quintiles 1-5 (Table 2); 4,233,824 in the full sample specification and 3,194,381 with the minimum 5 migrants restriction (Table 6); 13,951-147,284 pupils per subgroup-by-quintile educational choice regression (Table 4)
sample.n_individuals: roughly 400,000 pupils in the 2005-2011 cohorts; 297,771 pupils in the 2005-2009 descriptive sample (Table 3)

construction_notes: Teacher and exam scores are reported on the same grading scales; the grading scale was changed in 2008 and, for the descriptive tables, 2005-07 scores are converted to the new scale (possible scores 12/A, 10/B, 7/C, 4/D, 02/E, 00/Fx, -03/F).

For use in the regressions, scores are standardised to mean zero and standard deviation one; footnote 12 says this is done 'jointly within year and subject area' while p. 47 says it 'was applied to teacher and exam scores seperately within each year and subject'.

The dependent variable in the grading gap regressions is the difference between the standardised teacher score and the standardised exam score; Table 6 column 3 instead uses a binary indicator equal to one if the teacher score is equal to or greater than the exam score.
All subject-area scores enter with equal weight in the empirical analysis.

Parental education is classified into three categories: low (none or only one parent has high-school as the highest degree; 27%), high (both parents have some college education; 20%) and medium (the remaining 53%); high is the reference category.

Migrants are pupils whose both parents are born in non-Western countries (Western = EU-15, North America, Japan, Australia and New Zealand); third generation migrants and migrants from Western countries are counted as natives; 9% of pupils are migrants.
Ability is approximated by exam scores; regressions are run separately by exam-score quintile.
Second (final) term teacher scores are used to approximate the first-term teacher scores available at the time of application for post-compulsory education.
Standard errors in the grading gap regressions are corrected for clustering at the school level; Table 4 reports plain standard errors.
Missing value flags for all variables are included in the grading gap regressions with controls, but not shown (note to Table A2).

claims.statement: In the 1st (lowest) exam-score quintile, the teacher-exam grading gap of boys is -0.150 SD relative to girls, without further controls.

definition.value: Indicator for pupil gender (Male_i in Eq. (1)); the coefficient is the teacher-exam grading gap of boys relative to girls, girls being the reference group.

timing.value: Fixed pupil characteristic; grading gap measured at the end of grade 9 (cohorts graduating 2005-2011).

outcome.label: Grading gap: teacher score minus exam score (GR_ijTA - GR_ijEX)

definition.value: The difference between the teacher score and the exam score of pupil i in subject-area j in the grade 9 school-leaving certificate. Teacher and exam scores are standardised to mean zero and standard deviation one within year and subject area, so the gap is expressed in score standard deviations; the estimation sample includes only pupil-by-subject observations for which both a teacher and an exam score are available.

timing.value: End of grade 9: teacher scores are determined immediately before the exam period begins and the exam scores come from the school-leaving examinations at the end of grade 9.

units.value: standard deviations of the (standardised) teacher/exam score distribution

magnitude.interpretation: In short, I term this a 'grading gap against boys' of 0.15 SD.

estimand.target_population: Pupils in the 1st (lowest) quintile of the exam-score distribution among those completing grade 9 in Denmark in 2005-2011

population.description: Pupils in public and private schools (including efterskoler, excluding schools for pupils with special needs) completing grade 9 in 2005-2011; unit of observation is the pupil-by-subject-area observation with both a teacher and an exam score
population.selection: Only pupil-by-subject observations for which both teacher and exam scores are available; for the 2011 cohort, subjects assessed by national tests in grade 8 are excluded; estimated separately within exam-score quintiles

identification.source_of_variation: The data structure with two scores for each pupil and subject area - a subjective teacher score and an externally examined exam score - differenced across type of assessment on the one hand and across gender, parental education and ethnicity on the other

key_assumptions.assumption: Exam scores are a (more) objective measure of pupils' academic ability, so that the difference between teacher and exam scores of pupils with the same exam performance measures a grading disparity rather than a difference in ability.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 5.1 (Caveats) discusses two features of the exam scheme (oral exams; non-blind written exams) that make this approximation less than ideal and argues that both lead to under- rather than over-estimation of the gaps.

key_assumptions.assumption: Teacher and exam assessments are meant to measure the same set of skills, so that in the absence of grading disparities the difference between pupil groups would be the same under both assessment schemes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The 'Act on Public School' gives both assessments the same stated purpose; teacher scores must be determined before the exam period and must not reflect coursework or effort.

key_assumptions.assumption: Estimating separately by exam-score quintile makes pupils comparable in ability, taking account of between-group differences in grading disparities that emerge simply because groups sit at different locations on the achievement distribution (teacher grading is compensatory).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Raw data: average teacher grades plotted by exam scores show that pupils with low exam performance have higher teacher scores and vice versa.

implies_edges.from: exam-score quintile

key_assumptions.assumption: Linearity of the gap equation.

formal.as_written: GRi jTA - GRi jEX = α + γ · Malei + ∂ · ParEduci + δ · Migranti + β Xi + ui j

key_assumptions.assumption: Performance at the final exams does not influence the teacher scores, because teacher scores are determined immediately before the exam period begins.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The 'Act on Public School' requires final teacher scores to be set before the exam period; for the 2011 cohort, subjects where an external national test result was available to the teacher beforehand are excluded.

implies_edges.from: performance at the final exams

threats_discussed: Several exams are oral exams with both the teacher and an external examiner present, so oral exams are probably more prone to systematic assessment differences than written exams (Section 5.1).

Written exams are non-blind (pupil's and school's name are stated on the exam paper), so even exam scores may be susceptible to systematic disparities; the author argues this biases the estimated gaps downwards.

In some subjects the teacher and exam score pair does not cover exactly the same form of assessment (teacher scores cover oral and written assessment in one single score while exams are either written or oral).
Third generation migrants and migrants from Western countries are counted as natives, which the author notes 'might induce a downward bias in the estimated migrant grading gaps'.
Class and teacher fixed effects cannot be included because the data contain no class or teacher information, so within-school differences in grading practice across classes/teachers remain.
robustness_checks: Including ability (the exam score) directly as a continuous control and estimating on the full sample instead of splitting by ability quintile (Table 6, col. 2).
Linear probability model for the likelihood that the teacher score is equal to or greater than the exam score (Table 6, col. 3).
Excluding schools with fewer than five migrant pupils in the school-by-year cohort (Table 6, col. 4).
An alternative definition with more narrow categories for low and high parental education (footnote 15: 'yields nearly identical results').
unresolved_confounders: Systematic grading disparities in the exam scores themselves: exams are only partly remotely scored and are non-blind, which the author states cannot be accounted for ('While I cannot account for these flaws...') and which make the estimated gaps lower bounds.
Within-school differences in grading practice across classes and teachers, since the data contain no class or teacher information.

estimation.specification: Eq. (1): the gap between standardised teacher and exam scores regressed on a male indicator, parental education indicators (high = reference) and a migrant indicator, without further controls; estimated separately by exam-score quintile
controls: indicators for parental education (high, medium, low)
estimation.clustering: standard errors corrected for school-level clustering

heterogeneity.finding: The largest differences are in the middle of the achievement distribution and the smallest gap is found for high achievers (gaps against boys vary between roughly 0.1 and 0.2 SD).

heterogeneity.dimension: pupil group (gender / parental education / migrant background)
heterogeneity.finding: Overall, corrected grading gaps in specification 2 are largest by socioeconomic background and by gender, about 0.17 SD on average across quintiles, while grading gaps by migration status are smaller than both.

ambiguities: The paper documents grading disparities and explicitly does not claim to identify discrimination ('as I do not claim to be able to identify discrimination'); the graph edge records the tested pair, not a causal interpretation by the author.

prior_findings_compared.as_stated: If we average the by-subject results in Lavy (2008), the gender gap is -0.10 SD against boys, which is somewhat smaller than what I find.
On the other hand, Cornwell et al. (2013) finds a gender gap against boys that is somewhat larger: -0.22 SD.

threats_discussed: Several exams are oral exams with both the teacher and an external examiner present, so oral exams are probably more prone to systematic assessment differences than written exams (Section 5.1).

Written exams are non-blind (pupil's and school's name are stated on the exam paper), so even exam scores may be susceptible to systematic disparities; the author argues this biases the estimated gaps downwards.

In some subjects the teacher and exam score pair does not cover exactly the same form of assessment (teacher scores cover oral and written assessment in one single score while exams are either written or oral).
Third generation migrants and migrants from Western countries are counted as natives, which the author notes 'might induce a downward bias in the estimated migrant grading gaps'.
Class and teacher fixed effects cannot be included because the data contain no class or teacher information, so within-school differences in grading practice across classes/teachers remain.
robustness_checks: Including ability (the exam score) directly as a continuous control and estimating on the full sample instead of splitting by ability quintile (Table 6, col. 2).
Linear probability model for the likelihood that the teacher score is equal to or greater than the exam score (Table 6, col. 3).
Excluding schools with fewer than five migrant pupils in the school-by-year cohort (Table 6, col. 4).
An alternative definition with more narrow categories for low and high parental education (footnote 15: 'yields nearly identical results').
unresolved_confounders: Systematic grading disparities in the exam scores themselves: exams are only partly remotely scored and are non-blind, which the author states cannot be accounted for ('While I cannot account for these flaws...') and which make the estimated gaps lower bounds.
Within-school differences in grading practice across classes and teachers, since the data contain no class or teacher information.
